summary: Lists the requirements for a protocol that sets up the security keys for encrypted SIP media streams (SRTP). Beyond basic security needs, such a protocol must work smoothly with SIP. It also summarizes and compares the proposals that existed at the time.

plainLanguage.summary: Two people on a call need to agree on a secret code before they can scramble their voices. This note lists what a good way of agreeing on that code must do, and reviews the ideas people had proposed.

subtitle: A detailed requirements roadmap for securely negotiating SRTP keys in VoIP calls

tldr.problem: Secure RTP (SRTP) encrypts media streams, but endpoints must first agree on cryptographic keys. In SIP-based VoIP, this negotiation collides with real-world call scenarios like call forwarding (retargeting), ringing multiple phones (forking), and early media arrival, making secure key exchange far more complex than in traditional protocols.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5479 catalogs detailed requirements across three dimensions: the key management protocol itself (how to exchange keys safely), security properties (what attacks must be resisted), and operational needs (support for gateway termination, transcoding, call recording). The document also classifies threat models by attacker access to signaling and media paths.
tldr.outcome: A comprehensive requirements baseline for protocols like DTLS-SRTP and ZRTP, enabling consistent evaluation of key negotiation approaches. The requirements inform protocol design but do not mandate a single solution.

today: RFC 5479 remains the definitive requirements specification for SRTP key negotiation. While no single protocol satisfies every requirement equally, the document's framework has guided the development of DTLS-SRTP (widely deployed in WebRTC and enterprise VoIP), ZRTP (peer-to-peer), and other mechanisms. The requirements continue to shape discussions of VoIP security in new contexts such as encrypted conference calls and cloud-hosted PBX systems.

sections.title: Secure RTP and the Key Exchange Problem
sections.content:
Secure RTP (SRTP) encrypts and authenticates voice, video, and data streams using shared cryptographic keys. Before two endpoints can use SRTP, they must agree on these keys. In traditional network protocols, key exchange is straightforward: one endpoint generates keys, sends them to the peer, and both sides encrypt. But SIP (Session Initiation Protocol), which signals VoIP calls, introduces unusual scenarios that make key negotiation complex.

RFC 5479 does not propose a specific key negotiation mechanism. Instead, it lists requirements that any such mechanism must satisfy. These requirements arise from real call scenarios (call forwarding, incoming calls ringing multiple phones, early media, PSTN gateways) and security threats (passive eavesdropping, active message modification, key compromise). The document also surveys and compares existing proposals, categorizing them by where keys are exchanged (signaling path, media path, or both).

Understanding these requirements is essential for protocol designers, implementers, and anyone evaluating VoIP security solutions.
sections.plainLanguage: Making a secure call requires two people to pick a secret code before they talk. This document explains all the ways calls can go wrong and what a good method of picking codes must do.

sections.title: Call Scenarios That Complicate Key Exchange
sections.content:
Traditional security protocols are designed for simple client-server interactions. VoIP calls are messier. RFC 5479 identifies several call patterns that force designers to rethink key negotiation:

Clipping: In SIP's offer-answer model, a caller sends an SDP offer and may receive media from the callee before the SDP answer arrives (containing SRTP keys). If the key is not available, media is lost ("clipped"). The protocol must either provide keys early via SIP responses, or tolerate unencrypted early media.

Forking and retargeting: When a caller invites a SIP address (like alice@example.com), the call might be delivered to multiple phones (forking: Alice's desk phone, mobile, and laptop all ring), or redirected to another person (retargeting: the call is forwarded to Bob). Both scenarios require that only the endpoint that answers the call learns the SRTP keys. If all recipients of the initial invite receive keys, security is compromised.

Recording and transcoding: Some business environments require call recording or codec conversion by intermediate boxes. End-to-end SRTP encryption blocks these features unless the endpoints explicitly cooperate and share keys with the intermediary.

PSTN gateways: Calls may bridge VoIP and traditional phone networks. The gateway must decrypt SRTP on the VoIP side to interface with the PSTN, terminating end-to-end encryption.

Each scenario imposes specific demands on the key negotiation protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Real calls are messy. Your call might ring on five phones, be forwarded to someone else, start playing music before you answer, or need to record. Each of these situations changes how you should agree on a secret code.

sections.title: Threat Models and Security Requirements
sections.content:
RFC 5479 defines attack scenarios based on where an attacker can intercept traffic:

  • Signaling-path attacker: can see or modify SIP messages and the keys they carry.
  • Media-path attacker: can see or modify RTP/SRTP packets.
  • Both paths: can attack both signaling and media.

Each attacker type is classified as passive (eavesdropping only) or active (modifying messages). The RFC categorizes protocols into seven threat-resistance classes, ranked from weakest to strongest. For example, passive-signaling-passive-media means an attacker must eavesdrop on both paths to learn keys. active-signaling-active-media-detect means active attacks on both paths are required to compromise keys, and the endpoints can detect such attacks.

The document requires that key negotiation protocols support at least one mode offering the strongest class: active-signaling-active-media-detect. This ensures endpoints can always achieve end-to-end security if they choose, even in the face of sophisticated attackers.

Additional security requirements include support for perfect forward secrecy (old keys remain secret even if current keys leak), downgrade protection (attackers cannot force weaker cipher suites), and identity binding (keys are cryptographically tied to endpoint identities for use with SIP Identity signatures).
sections.plainLanguage: An attacker might be listening to phone calls, modifying the secret codes sent between phones, or both. A good protocol must be able to defend against any of these threats, so you can pick how much security you want.

sections.title: Requirements for the Key Management Protocol
sections.content:
RFC 5479 lists detailed requirements the key negotiation protocol must satisfy:

Handling SIP's complexity: The protocol must support secure forking and retargeting, ensuring non-answering endpoints do not learn session keys. It must function even if SIP proxies selectively discard error messages (the HERFP problem). It should avoid media clipping and allow association between SIP signaling messages and key negotiation messages, so endpoints can verify they are talking to the right party.

Negotiation: Each session MUST allow independent negotiation of security parameters (cipher suites, algorithms). The protocol must prevent a two-time pad (the same key and RTP SSRC used by two senders), which would compromise confidentiality.

Performance and reuse: The protocol MAY support reuse of previously negotiated security contexts to reduce setup latency on resource-constrained devices (handsets, gateways).

Compatibility: The protocol must work across different signaling approaches: pure SIP, SIP with non-SIP endpoints (H.323, MGCP), and situations where some endpoints support SRTP while others only support unencrypted RTP.

Media path considerations: If key negotiation happens over the media path (on the same UDP ports as RTP), negotiation packets must be distinguishable from RTP packets (by failing the RTP validity check).
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol must handle phones being forwarded, multiple rings, weak devices, interworking with old protocols, and situations where not everyone wants to use SRTP.

sections.title: Deployment Realities and Operational Considerations
sections.content:
Beyond pure security and protocol mechanics, RFC 5479 addresses real-world constraints:

Certificates: Many endpoints cannot obtain X.509 certificates from certificate authorities. The protocol must support authentication without requiring end-users to source credentials from a third party. Self-signed certificates or other methods (pre-shared keys, out-of-band verification) are essential.

Algorithm agility: The protocol must support multiple cipher suites and allow introducing new algorithms without breaking deployed implementations. This is critical as cryptographic standards evolve.

Denial of service: The protocol must not inadvertently allow attackers to exhaust endpoints with CPU-intensive operations (e.g., forcing expensive Diffie-Hellman calculations from unauthenticated sources).

FIPS compliance: U.S. federal agencies and many enterprises require algorithms validated under FIPS 140-2. The protocol should support such algorithms.

Interoperability: When endpoints use different key management mechanisms (one uses MIKEY-RSA, another DTLS-SRTP), interworking is necessary but challenging without decryption/re-encryption in the middle.

The RFC's appendices catalog existing approaches (MIKEY variants, SDP Security Descriptions, ZRTP, DTLS-SRTP, EKT) and evaluate them against both SIP-specific and security criteria, providing designers and operators with a comparative baseline.
sections.plainLanguage: Phones don't have fancy certificate stores. New encryption methods will be invented. Attackers will try to slow things down. A good protocol handles all this, and works even when people use different software.
